public class SnowflakeIdGenerator {
    private final long workerId;
    private long sequence = 0L;
    private long lastTimestamp = -1L;

    public SnowflakeIdGenerator(long workerId) {
        if (workerId < 0 || workerId > 31) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        this.workerId = workerId;
    }

    public synchronized long nextId() {
        long timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (timestamp < lastTimestamp) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Clock moved backwards!");
        }
        if (timestamp == lastTimestamp) {
            sequence = (sequence + 1) & 4095L; // 12-bit
            if (sequence == 0) {
                while (System.currentTimeMillis() <= lastTimestamp);
                timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis();
            }
        } else {
            sequence = 0L;
        }
        lastTimestamp = timestamp;
        return (timestamp << 22) | (workerId << 12) | sequence;
    }
}

For production environments, recommend using: Meituan Leaf, Baidu UidGenerator.

5. Snowflake + Redis (Solving Clock Rollback)

Advantages

  • Retains the high-performance advantages of Snowflake.
  • Uses Redis to record the most recent timestamp, preventing ID duplication caused by clock rollback.
  • More secure and reliable, suitable for strongly consistent scenarios.

Disadvantages

  • Dependent on Redis, increasing system complexity.
  • Each generation requires reading/writing Redis, slightly reduced performance.
  • Requires designing a fallback strategy (e.g., falling back to UUID).

Suitable Scenarios

  • Systems that absolutely cannot tolerate ID duplication, such as finance, payment, and accounting systems.

Pseudocode Logic

public long safeNextId(SnowflakeIdGenerator snowflake) {
    String key = "snowflake:last_time";
    Long lastTime = redis.opsForValue().get(key) != null ?
        Long.parseLong(redis.opsForValue().get(key)) : 0L;

    long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
    if (now < lastTime) {
        // Clock rollback! Activate fallback plan
        return fallbackToUUID(); // Or throw an exception
    }

    long id = snowflake.nextId();
    redis.opsForValue().set(key, String.valueOf(now), Duration.ofDays(365));
    return id;
}

6. Timestamp + Redis Sequence (Custom Composite ID)

Advantages

  • Assemble your own ID, free format.
  • Roughly ordered + globally unique: e.g., 1712345678901000123.
  • Independent counter per millisecond, avoiding conflicts.
  • ID carries time information, making troubleshooting easier.

Disadvantages

  • ID is relatively long (typically >18 digits), requires BIGINT or string storage.
  • Dependent on Redis, requires an operation per millisecond.
  • Must set key expiration to prevent memory explosion.

Suitable Scenarios

  • When you want a “Snowflake-like” effect but do not want to assign worker IDs.
  • When you need readable IDs with embedded timestamps.

Code Example 

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
9

public String generateOrderId() {
    long timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis();
    String key = "order:id:seq:" + timestamp;

    Long seq = redis.opsForValue().increment(key);
    redis.expire(key, 24, TimeUnit.HOURS); // Expire after 24 hours

    return timestamp + String.format("%06d", seq); // e.g., 1712345678901000123
}

Comparison Summary of the Six Approaches

Approach Ordered Readable Performance Distributed-Friendly Complexity Recommended Scenario
MySQL Auto-Increment Yes Yes Medium (DB-dependent) Difficult with sharding Low Monolithic small projects
UUID No No High Yes Low Tokens, temporary IDs
Redis INCR Yes Yes Very High Yes Low Small-medium systems with Redis
Snowflake (Pure) Roughly ordered Yes Very High Yes Medium High-concurrency distributed
Snowflake + Redis Roughly ordered Yes High Strong consistency Medium-High Finance, payments
Timestamp + Redis Sequence Roughly ordered Yes High Yes Low Custom ID format

Final Recommendations

  • Early-stage projects: Use MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT or Redis INCR — simple and sufficient.
  • When scaling up: Switch to Snowflake (recommend using Leaf or UidGenerator).
  • Never use UUID as a primary key! Unless you truly do not care about insertion performance.
  • ID design should consider the future: Will you shard databases? Will information be exposed? Is sorting required?

item.title: JWT Explained: Principles, Implementation, and Best Practices
item.description:
User Login Authentication Flow (Based on JWT)

  1. The user enters their username and password and sends them to the server via an HTTPS request.

  2. The server verifies the credentials:

    • If verification succeeds, it generates a signed JWT (JSON Web Token) and returns it to the client;
    • If verification fails, it returns an error message.

  3. After the client (e.g., a browser) receives the JWT, it stores it (typically in localStorage or cookie; for Vue.js frameworks, Vuex or Pinia can be used).

  4. For every subsequent request, the client includes the JWT in the HTTP request header (e.g., Authorization: Bearer <token>) and sends it to the server.

  5. Upon receiving the request, the server:

    • Uses its locally stored secret key to verify the JWT signature;
    • If the signature is valid and the token has not expired (determined by the exp field), the user is considered authenticated and the requested data is returned;
    • Otherwise, the request is rejected.

  6. When the user logs out, the client simply destroys the locally stored token — the server does not need to take any action.

Introduction to JWT

JWT (JSON Web Token) is an open standard (RFC 7519) for securely transmitting information between parties as a JSON object. It encrypts/encodes user information (such as user ID, roles, etc.) into the token’s payload, and the server does not store any user information. The server verifies the correctness of the token using the stored secret key — if it is correct, authentication passes.

Its advantages include solving single sign-on problems well in distributed systems and easily resolving session sharing issues. JWT is relatively short in length and can be transmitted via URL (URL-safe).

Core Characteristics:

  • Stateless: The server does not store session information; all authentication data is contained within the token.
  • Self-contained: The token itself carries the necessary data, reducing database queries.
  • Cross-domain and Distributed System Support: Naturally suited for microservice architectures and Single Sign-On (SSO) scenarios.
  • URL-safe: Base64Url encoding allows it to be safely transmitted via URL, POST parameters, or HTTP Headers.

JWT Generation Example (Java)

/** Generate token */
public static String generateToken(Map<String, Object> claimMaps) {

    if (null != claimMaps) {
        claimMaps.forEach((key, val) -> {
            claimMaps.put(key, val.toString());
        });
    }

    return Jwts.builder()
            // JWT_ID, can be used for unique identification of each signature
            .setId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
            // Data compression method
            .compressWith(CompressionCodecs.GZIP)
            // Issuer information
            .setIssuer(ISSUER)
            // Subject
            .setSubject("system")
            // Audience
            .setAudience(AUDIENCE)
            // Issued-at timestamp
            .setIssuedAt(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis()))
            // Expiration timestamp
            .setExpiration(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis() + EXPIRES_IN * 1000))
            // Claim information, custom payload
            .addClaims(claimMaps)
            // Signature algorithm + secret key
            .signWith(SIGNATURE_ALGORITHM, secretKey)
            .compact();
}

The process of verifying a token is essentially the same as generating a new token.

Based on the received header, payload, and the secret key stored on the server, a new token is regenerated and compared:

  • If the tokens match, the token is valid and has not been tampered with.
  • If the token has not been tampered with, the payload can be further decrypted via Base64, and the exp expiration field in the payload can be used to determine whether the token has expired.

Note: JWT itself contains authentication information, so once the information is leaked, anyone can obtain all the permissions of the token. Therefore, when doing front-end development, it is best not to store JWT in Cookie, which is a storage unit prone to leaking personal privacy information.

Advantages

  • Stateless & Scalable: Very suitable for distributed systems and microservice architectures;
  • Solves Session Sharing Issues: No need to share session storage;
  • Natively supports cross-domain and mobile;
  • Reduces database pressure: Authentication information is built into the token, eliminating the need for frequent database queries.

Disadvantages and Risks

  1. Cannot actively revoke tokens Once issued, a token remains valid until it expires. If a user logs out or their permissions change, the server cannot immediately invalidate the old token (unless a blacklist mechanism is introduced, but this goes against the stateless design principle).
  2. Risk of sensitive information leakage Although the Payload is Base64-encoded, it is not encrypted (unless JWE is used). Never store sensitive data such as passwords in the token.
  3. HTTPS is mandatory JWT is transmitted over the network. If HTTP is used, it is highly susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks. Always use HTTPS throughout.
  4. Large token size Compared to traditional session IDs, JWT is longer because it contains data, which may affect performance (especially in high-frequency request scenarios).

Additional Notes

  • Single Sign-On (SSO): JWT natively supports SSO because the token can be verified by multiple services.

  • Homepage Access Control: If you need to “open the homepage” (i.e., allow anonymous access), you should configure a whitelist path in the gateway or interceptor to skip JWT verification.

  • Cross-domain Support: JWT itself is not related to CORS, but when used with the Authorization Header, cross-domain authentication can be easily achieved.

  • Comparison with Spring Session:

    • Spring Session relies on server-side storage (e.g., Redis) and supports active invalidation;
    • JWT is stateless but sacrifices real-time control capability;
    • Both are suitable for different scenarios and can be used in combination (e.g., using JWT for authentication and Redis for managing blacklists).

Recommended Approaches for Enhancing JWT Security and Controllability

Although JWT has advantages such as being stateless and scalable, its characteristic of “inability to actively revoke” does pose challenges in certain business scenarios (such as user logout, password changes, permission changes). To address this, the following two complementary strategies are recommended to enhance the system’s security control capabilities:

Approach 1: Short-lived Access Token + Refresh Token Mechanism

  • Core Idea:

    • Access Token: Has a short validity period (e.g., 15–30 minutes), used for everyday API authentication;
    • Refresh Token: Has a longer validity period (e.g., 7 days), stored in a secure HttpOnly Cookie or secure storage, used only to obtain a new Access Token.

  • Workflow:

    1. After the user successfully logs in, the server returns a pair of tokens: access_token and refresh_token;
    2. The client uses the access_token to call protected APIs;
    3. When the access_token expires, the client uses the refresh_token to request a new access_token from the authentication service;
    4. If the user logs out or changes their password, the server immediately revokes the corresponding refresh_token (e.g., deletes it from the database or Redis);
    5. Even if the old access_token has not yet expired, since it cannot be renewed, the effective window is greatly shortened.

  • Advantages:

    • Balances security and user experience;
    • After logout, the token becomes fully invalid at most after one Access Token lifecycle (e.g., 30 minutes);
    • Conforms to OAuth 2.0 standard practices.

Approach 2: Lightweight Token Blacklist / Whitelist Mechanism Based on Redis

  • Implementation A: JTI Blacklist

    • Embed a unique identifier in the JWT’s jti (JWT ID) field;
    • When a user logs out, changes password, or has permission changes, store the jti and its expiration time in Redis (TTL = remaining validity period of the original JWT);
    • Each time a JWT is verified, additionally check whether the jti exists in the blacklist;
    • If it exists, reject the request.

  • Implementation B: User Session Whitelist (Stricter)

    • After each successful login generates a JWT, store the full token string (or its hash value) in Redis keyed by user_id:session_id;
    • All protected APIs, after verifying the JWT signature and expiration, additionally verify whether the token exists in Redis;
    • When a user logs out, changes password, or an administrator forces an offline, delete the corresponding Redis key;
    • At this point, even if the token has not expired and the signature is valid, it will be rejected because it is “not in the whitelist.”

  • Advantages:

    • Achieves true instant logout;
    • Supports fine-grained control (e.g., multi-device management, forced logout);
    • Redis offers high performance with minimal impact on system throughput.

  • Notes:

    • Properly set the TTL of Redis keys to avoid unlimited memory growth;
    • While the whitelist approach is more secure, it slightly sacrifices JWT’s “fully stateless” nature, belonging to a stateful enhancement pattern.

Comprehensive Recommendations

Scenario Recommended Approach
General Web applications, mobile Apps Access Token + Refresh Token (balances security and performance)
High-security systems (e.g., finance, admin panels) Refresh Token + Redis Blacklist/Whitelist
Need to support “multi-device login management” Use Redis Whitelist + session_id to identify devices

💡 Best Practice: Even when using a blacklist mechanism, keep the Access Token’s validity period short (e.g., ≤30 minutes) to limit Redis storage pressure and potential attack windows.

Introduction to ThreadLocal

From the description in the official Java documentation: The ThreadLocal class is used to provide thread-local variables. Such variables, when accessed in a multi-threaded environment (via get and set methods), ensure that each thread’s variables remain relatively independent from variables in other threads. ThreadLocal instances are typically private static fields, used to associate threads with their thread context.

We can deduce that the purpose of ThreadLocal is: to provide local variables within a thread, ensuring different threads do not interfere with each other. These variables are effective throughout the thread’s lifecycle, reducing the complexity of passing common variables between multiple functions or components within the same thread.

  • Thread concurrency: In multi-threaded concurrent scenarios
  • Passing data: We can use ThreadLocal to pass common variables between different components within the same thread (somewhat similar to Session?)
  • Thread isolation: Each thread’s variables are independent and do not affect each other

Basic Usage

Differences Between ThreadLocal and Synchronized

Although both the ThreadLocal pattern and the Synchronized keyword are used to handle the problem of multi-threaded concurrent access to variables, their approaches and perspectives differ.

Synchronized ThreadLocal
Principle The synchronization mechanism uses a time-for-space tradeoff, providing only one copy of the variable and having different threads queue for access ThreadLocal uses a space-for-time tradeoff, providing each thread with its own copy of the variable, enabling simultaneous access without interference
Focus Synchronization of resource access among multiple threads Data isolation between threads in a multi-threaded environment

Summary: In the example above, although both ThreadLocal and Synchronized can solve the problem, using ThreadLocal is more appropriate because it allows the program to have higher concurrency.

Use Cases

Through the introduction above, we have basically understood the characteristics of ThreadLocal. But in what specific scenarios is it used? Let us look at an example: transaction operations.

Transfer Example

Let us first build a simple transfer scenario: there is a data table account with two users, Jack and Rose. User Jack transfers money to user Rose. The implementation mainly uses a MySQL database, JDBC, and the C3P0 framework. Below is the detailed code:

Introducing Transactions

Important considerations when starting transactions:

To ensure all operations are within a single transaction, the connection used in the example must be the same one. The connection opened at the service layer for the transaction must be consistent with the connection used by the DAO layer to access the database.

In a multi-threaded concurrent scenario, each thread can only operate its own connection — that is, thread isolation.

Conventional Solution

Based on the premises given above, the solutions people typically think of are:

  • Pass the connection object from the service layer to the DAO layer
  • Use locking

Drawbacks of the Conventional Solution

  • Increases code coupling (because we need to pass the connection parameter from the service layer)
  • Reduces program performance (adding synchronized code blocks sacrifices concurrency)

At this point, ThreadLocal can be used to bind the connection to the current thread, reducing coupling between code.

Solving with ThreadLocal

In response to the above situation, we need to modify the original JDBC connection pool object:

  • Instead of fetching objects from the connection pool directly, fetch the connection object bound to the current thread
  • If the connection object is null:
    • Fetch a connection from the connection pool
    • Bind this connection object to the current thread

ThreadLocal<Connection> tl = new ThreadLocal();
public static Connection getConnection() {
    Connection conn = tl.get();
    if(conn == null) {
        conn = ds.getConnection();
        tl.set(conn);
    }
    return conn;
}

Benefits of the ThreadLocal Approach

From the above example, we can see that in certain specific scenarios, the ThreadLocal approach has two prominent advantages:

  • Passing data: Save data bound to each thread, which can be directly retrieved where needed, avoiding the code coupling issues caused by direct parameter passing
  • Thread isolation: Data between threads is mutually isolated while maintaining concurrency, avoiding the performance loss caused by synchronization

Internal Structure of ThreadLocal

Through the above learning, we have gained some understanding of ThreadLocal’s functionality. Now let us look at ThreadLocal’s internal structure together and explore the principles behind its ability to achieve thread data isolation.

Common Misconception

If we do not read the source code, we might guess that ThreadLocal is designed like this: each ThreadLocal creates a Map, then uses Thread as the Map’s key and the local variable to be stored as the Map’s value. This way, the effect of isolating local variables for each thread is achieved. This is the simplest design, and indeed, the earliest versions of ThreadLocal in the JDK were designed this way — but not anymore.

The Current Design

However, the JDK later optimized the design. In JDK 8, ThreadLocal’s design is: each Thread maintains a ThreadLocalMap, where the Map’s key is the ThreadLocal instance itself, and the value is the actual Object to be stored. The specific process is as follows:

  • Each Thread has a Map (ThreadLocalMap) internally
  • The Map stores ThreadLocal objects (as keys) and the thread’s variable copies (as values)
  • The Map inside Thread is maintained by ThreadLocal, which is responsible for getting and setting the thread’s variable values from/to the Map
  • For different threads, each time a copy value is retrieved, other threads cannot access the current thread’s copy value, thus forming copy isolation with no mutual interference

Comparison

What are the benefits of the JDK 8 design change?

  • The number of Entries stored in each Map is reduced, because originally the number of Entries was determined by the number of Threads, whereas now it is determined by the number of ThreadLocals.
    • In real development, the number of Threads far exceeds the number of ThreadLocals.
  • When a Thread is destroyed, its ThreadLocalMap is also destroyed along with it, because ThreadLocalMap is stored within Thread and disappears as Thread is destroyed, reducing overhead.

Source Code Analysis of ThreadLocal Core Methods

Based on ThreadLocal’s internal structure, let us continue to analyze the source code of its core methods for a deeper understanding of its operating principles. Apart from the constructor, ThreadLocal exposes the following 4 methods:

Method Declaration Description
protected T initialValue() Returns the initial value of the current thread’s local variable
public void set(T value) Sets the local variable bound to the current thread
public T get() Gets the local variable bound to the current thread
public void remove() Removes the local variable bound to the current thread

Below is a detailed source code analysis of these 4 methods. (To keep the thought process clear, the ThreadLocalMap part will not be expanded for now — it will be detailed in the next section.)

The set Method

Code flow:

  • First, obtain the current thread, and based on the current thread, obtain a Map
  • If the obtained Map is not empty, set the parameter into the Map (using the current ThreadLocal’s reference as the key)
  • If the Map is empty, create a Map for this thread and set the initial value

The get Method

Code execution flow:

  • First, obtain the current thread, and based on the current thread, obtain a Map
  • If the obtained Map is not empty, use the ThreadLocal’s reference as the key to get the corresponding Entry from the Map. Otherwise, go to step 4
  • If the Entry is not null, return e.value. Otherwise, go to step 4
  • If the Map is empty or the Entry is null, obtain the initial value through the initialValue function, then use the ThreadLocal’s reference and the value as firstKey and firstValue to create a new Map

Summary: First, get the ThreadLocal variable of the current thread. If it exists, return the value; if not, create it and return the initial value.

The remove Method

Code execution flow:

  • First, obtain the current thread, and based on the current thread, obtain a Map
  • If the obtained Map is not empty, remove the Entry corresponding to the current ThreadLocal object

The initialValue Method

The purpose of this method is to return the initial value of this thread’s local variable.

  • This method is a lazily invoked method. From the code above, we know it is executed only when set has not yet been called but get is called first, and it executes only once.
  • The default implementation directly returns null.
  • If you want an initial value other than null, you can override this method. (Note: This method is protected, clearly designed to be overridden by subclasses.)

When analyzing ThreadLocal’s methods, we learned that ThreadLocal’s operations are essentially carried out around ThreadLocalMap. The source code of ThreadLocalMap is relatively complex. We will discuss it from the following three aspects.

Basic Structure

In ThreadLocalMap, Entry is also used to store K-V structure data. However, the key in Entry can only be a ThreadLocal object, which is already constrained in the constructor.

Furthermore, Entry extends WeakReference, meaning the key (ThreadLocal) is a weak reference. Its purpose is to decouple the lifecycle of the ThreadLocal object from the thread lifecycle.

Weak References and Memory Leaks

Some developers encounter memory leaks while using ThreadLocal and conjecture that the leak is related to the use of weak references for the key in Entry. This understanding is actually incorrect.

Let us first review several conceptual terms involved in this problem, then analyze the issue.

Memory Leak Related Concepts

Memory overflow: There is not enough memory available for the requester to use.

Memory leak: Refers to heap memory that has been dynamically allocated by a program but, for some reason, is not released or cannot be released, resulting in wasted system memory, leading to slowed program execution speed or even system crashes. The accumulation of memory leaks will eventually lead to memory overflow.

Weak Reference Related Concepts

There are 4 types of references in Java: strong, soft, weak, and phantom. The current issue primarily involves strong and weak references:

Strong Reference (“Strong” Reference) is the most common ordinary object reference we encounter. As long as a strong reference points to an object, it indicates that the object is still “alive”, and the garbage collector will not reclaim such an object.

Weak Reference (WeakReference): Once the garbage collector discovers an object that only has weak references, it will reclaim its memory regardless of whether the current memory space is sufficient.

Would a memory leak occur if the key used strong references?

Suppose the key in ThreadLocalMap used strong references — would a memory leak occur?

At this point, the memory diagram for ThreadLocal (solid lines indicate strong references) is as follows:

  • Suppose after using ThreadLocal in business code, the threadLocal Ref is reclaimed.
  • But because the ThreadLocalMap’s Entry holds a strong reference to threadLocal, threadLocal cannot be reclaimed.
  • Without manually deleting this Entry and with the CurrentThread still running, there is always a strong reference chain threadRef -> currentThread -> threadLocalMap -> entry, and the Entry will not be reclaimed (the Entry includes the ThreadLocal instance and value), causing an Entry memory leak.

In other words, if the key in ThreadLocalMap uses strong references, memory leaks cannot be completely avoided.

Would a memory leak occur if the key uses weak references?

  • Similarly, suppose after using ThreadLocal in business code, the threadLocal Ref is reclaimed.
  • Since ThreadLocalMap only holds a weak reference to ThreadLocal, with no strong references pointing to the threadlocal instance, threadlocal can be smoothly reclaimed by the GC. At this point, the key in the Entry = null.
  • However, without manually deleting this Entry and with the CurrentThread still running, there also exists a strong reference chain threadRef -> currentThread -> threadLocalMap -> entry -> value, so value will not be reclaimed, and this piece of value will never be accessible again, causing a value memory leak.

In other words, even if the key in ThreadLocalMap uses weak references, memory leaks are still possible.

The Real Cause of Memory Leaks

Comparing the two cases above, we find that the occurrence of memory leaks has nothing to do with whether the key in ThreadLocalMap uses weak references. So what is the real cause of memory leaks?

Careful readers will notice that in both memory leak scenarios above, there are two prerequisites:

  • The Entry was not manually deleted
  • The CurrentThread is still running

The first point is easy to understand: as long as you call the remove method to delete the corresponding Entry after using ThreadLocal, memory leaks can be avoided.

The second point is slightly more complex. Since ThreadLocalMap is an attribute of Thread and is referenced by the current thread, its lifecycle is as long as the Thread’s. So after using ThreadLocal, if the current Thread also finishes execution, ThreadLocalMap will naturally be reclaimed by the GC, avoiding memory leaks at the root.

In summary, the root cause of ThreadLocal memory leaks is: because the lifecycle of ThreadLocalMap is as long as the Thread’s, failure to manually delete the corresponding key will lead to memory leaks.

Why Use Weak References?

Based on the analysis just now, we know: regardless of which type of reference is used for the key in ThreadLocalMap, memory leaks cannot be completely avoided. It has nothing to do with using weak references.

There are two ways to avoid memory leaks:

  • After using ThreadLocal, call its remove method to delete the corresponding Entry
  • After using ThreadLocal, the current Thread also finishes execution

Compared to the first approach, the second is clearly harder to control, especially when using thread pools — threads that finish executing are not destroyed but instead returned to the thread pool.

That is to say, as long as you remember to call remove promptly after using ThreadLocal, there will be no problem regardless of whether the key is a strong or weak reference. So why use weak references for the key?

In fact, in the set/getEntry methods of ThreadLocalMap, a check is performed for keys that are null (i.e., ThreadLocal being null). If null, the value is set to null.

This means that after using ThreadLocal, even if the CurrentThread is still running and you forget to call the remove method, weak references provide one extra layer of protection compared to strong references: the weakly referenced ThreadLocal will be reclaimed, and the corresponding value will be cleared the next time any of ThreadLocalMap’s set, get, or remove methods is called, thereby avoiding memory leaks.

Hash Conflict Resolution

Hash conflict resolution is an important topic in Map implementations. Let us use hash conflict resolution as a thread to study the core source code of ThreadLocalMap.

First, let us start from ThreadLocal’s set method:

public void set(T value) {
    Thread t = Thread.currentThread();
    ThreadLocal.ThreadLocalMap map = getMap(t);
    if (map != null)
        // Calls ThreadLocalMap's set method
        map.set(this, value);
    else
        createMap(t, value);
}

ThreadLocal.ThreadLocalMap getMap(Thread t) {
    return t.threadLocals;
}

void createMap(Thread t, T firstValue) {
    // Calls ThreadLocalMap's constructor
    t.threadLocals = new ThreadLocal.ThreadLocalMap(this, firstValue);
}

We analyzed this method earlier. Its purpose is to set the local variable bound to the current thread:

  • First, obtain the current thread, and based on the current thread, obtain a Map
  • If the obtained Map is not empty, set the parameter into the Map (using the current ThreadLocal’s reference as the key) (this calls ThreadLocalMap’s set method)
  • If the Map is empty, create a Map for this thread and set the initial value (this calls ThreadLocalMap’s constructor)

This code touches on two methods of ThreadLocalMap in two places. Let us analyze these two methods next.

Constructor

ThreadLocalMap(ThreadLocal<?> firstKey, Object firstValue)

The constructor first creates an Entry array of length 16, then calculates the index corresponding to firstKey, stores it in the table, and sets the size and threshold.

Key analysis: int i = firstKey.threadLocalHashCode & (INITIAL_CAPACITY - 1)

About: threadLocalHashCode

An AtomicInteger type is defined here. Each time the current value is obtained and HASH_INCREMENT is added. HASH_INCREMENT = 0x61c88647, a value related to the Fibonacci sequence (golden ratio). Its main purpose is to allow hash codes to be evenly distributed across an array whose length is a power of 2 — that is, in the Entry[] table. Doing so minimizes hash conflicts.

About: & (INITIAL_CAPACITY - 1)

When computing the hash, the algorithm hashCode & (size - 1) is used internally. This is a more efficient implementation equivalent to the modulo operation hashCode % size. It is precisely because of this algorithm that we require size to be a power of 2, which also ensures that the number of hash conflicts is reduced while the index does not go out of bounds.

The set Method (of ThreadLocalMap)

Code execution flow:

  • First, calculate index i based on the key, then look up the Entry at that position
  • If the Entry already exists and the key equals the passed-in key, then directly assign the new value to this Entry
  • If the Entry exists but the key is null, call replaceStaleEntry to replace this Entry whose key is null
  • Continuously loop until a null position is encountered. If no return occurs during the loop, create a new Entry at this null position, insert it, and increment size by 1

Finally, call cleanSomeSlots to clean up Entries with null keys. Then check whether sz >= threshold, meaning the rehash condition is met. If so, call the rehash function to perform a full-table scan cleanup.

Linear Probing for Hash Conflict Resolution

This method probes subsequent addresses one by one until an empty address is found for insertion. If no empty address is found in the entire space, an overflow occurs.

For example, suppose the current table length is 16. If the hash value calculated for the key is 14 and table[14] already has a value whose key does not match the current key, then a hash conflict has occurred. At this point, add 1 to 14 to get 15 and check table[15]. If still a conflict, wrap around back to 0 and check table[0], and so on, until an insertion point is found.

Following the description above, the Entry table can be viewed as a circular array.

ThreadLocal Use Cases

Use Cases in Source Code

The primary role of ThreadLocal is data isolation. The data it stores belongs only to the current thread, and the variable data is relatively isolated from other threads. In a multi-threaded environment, it prevents one’s variables from being tampered with by other threads.

For example, the source code used by Spring to implement transaction isolation levels:

Spring uses ThreadLocal to ensure that database operations within a single thread use the same database connection. At the same time, this approach allows the business layer to use transactions without needing to be aware of or manage connection objects. Through propagation levels, it skillfully manages switching, suspending, and resuming among multiple transaction configurations.

The Spring framework uses ThreadLocal to achieve this isolation, primarily in the TransactionSynchronizationManager class, as shown in the code below:

 1
 2
 3
 4
 5

 9
10

private static final Log logger = LogFactory.getLog(TransactionSynchronizationManager.class);

    private static final ThreadLocal<Map<Object, Object>> resources =
            new NamedThreadLocal<>("Transactional resources");

    private static final ThreadLocal<Set<TransactionSynchronization>> synchronizations =
            new NamedThreadLocal<>("Transaction synchronizations");

    private static final ThreadLocal<String> currentTransactionName =
            new NamedThreadLocal<>("Current transaction name");

Spring’s transactions are primarily implemented through ThreadLocal and AOP. I mention this here so that everyone knows each thread’s own connection is stored via ThreadLocal.

User Scenario 1

Beyond source code scenarios, do you have your own use cases for ThreadLocal?

Previously, after going live, we discovered that dates for some users were incorrect. After investigation, it turned out to be a SimpleDateFormat issue. At the time, we used SimpleDateFormat’s parse() method, which internally has a Calendar object. Calling SimpleDateFormat’s parse() method first calls Calendar.clear() and then Calendar.add(). If one thread calls add() first and then another thread calls clear(), the time parsed by parse() will be incorrect.

In fact, solving this problem is very simple — let each thread create its own SimpleDateFormat. But would 1000 threads need to create 1000 SimpleDateFormat instances?

So at the time, we used a thread pool combined with ThreadLocal to wrap SimpleDateFormat, then overrode initialValue so each thread had its own copy of SimpleDateFormat. This solved the thread safety issue while also improving performance.

User Scenario 2

In my project, there was a thread frequently encountering the need to pass objects across several method calls — the context. It is a state, often representing user identity, task information, etc., leading to the problem of excessive parameter passing.

Using something like the Chain of Responsibility pattern, adding a context parameter to each method is very cumbersome. Moreover, sometimes when the call chain involves third-party libraries whose source code cannot be modified, the object parameter cannot be passed in. So I used ThreadLocal to refactor this. Now, you only need to set the parameter in ThreadLocal before the call, and elsewhere just get it.

void work(User user) {
    getInfo(user);
    checkInfo(user);
    setSomeThing(user);

void work(User user) {
try{
      threadLocalUser.set(user);

    getInfo();

     threadLocalUser.remove();

}

I have seen that in many scenarios, data isolation for cookies, sessions, etc., is implemented using ThreadLocal.

In Android, the Looper class leverages ThreadLocal’s characteristics to ensure each thread has only one Looper object.

Why Use Scoop

Scoop official website

On Windows, setting up a development environment has always been a complex and challenging problem. Without a unified standard, the installation methods for various development tools differ drastically, incurring a lot of unnecessary time costs. Scoop helps you install and manage common development software in a unified way, saving you the tedious steps of manually downloading installers and configuring environment variables.

For example, installing Python and Node.js only requires:

1
2

scoop install python
scoop install nodejs

Installing Scoop

Personally tested + official installation method

Install the latest version of PowerShell from the Microsoft Store

Open PowerShell and enter the following commands

1
2

Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri https://get.scoop.sh | Invoke-Expression

If you see the image below, the installation is successful

Scoop requires Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell as its runtime. If you are using Windows 10 or above, Windows PowerShell is built into the system. However, the built-in Windows PowerShell on Windows 7 is too outdated, so you will need to manually install a newer version of PowerShell.

As many users set their Windows username in Chinese, the user directory also ends up with a Chinese name. If software is installed under the user directory using Scoop’s default settings, it may cause execution errors for some software. Therefore, it is recommended to install to a custom directory. For other installation methods, please refer to: ScoopInstaller/Install

1
2
3
4
5
6

# Set PowerShell execution policy
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser
# Download install script
irm get.scoop.sh -outfile 'install.ps1'
# Run installation, --ScoopDir parameter specifies the Scoop installation path
.\install.ps1 -ScoopDir 'C:\Scoop'

Using Scoop

Scoop’s official documentation is very beginner-friendly. Rather than repeating it here, we recommend reading the official documentation or the Quick Start guide.

Common Commands

Command Purpose
scoop bucket list List all buckets installed
scoop search Search for software
scoop install Install software
scoop list View installed software
scoop uninstall Uninstall software
scoop bucket Manage buckets
scoop update Update software
scoop config proxy Set proxy for Scoop
scoop reset Switch software versions

Q&A

Can Scoop be configured to use a mirror source?

The Scoop community only maintains installation configurations. All software is downloaded from the official download links provided by the software vendors, so mirror sources are not available. If your network environment causes repeated download failures, you may need a bit of magic.

Why can’t I find Java 8?

The reason is the same as above. The vendor no longer provides download links for Java 8. It is recommended to use ojdkbuild8 as an alternative.

How do I install Python 2?

For deprecated and discontinued software, the Scoop community removes it from ScoopInstaller/Main and adds it to ScoopInstaller/Versions. If you need such software, you must manually add the bucket:

1
2

scoop bucket add versions
scoop install python27
